### [2026-09-05] P5-T09 — Notification bell/list UI + full-suite hang investigation and fix — frontend-builder

**Context:** picked up mid-flight. A prior frontend-builder session built P5-T09's actual feature
code (`notification-bell.tsx`, `notification-reason-meta.ts`, `notifications.ts`, the `AppHeader`
wiring) but stalled twice before ever appending a MEMORY.md entry or confirming the full suite
green — the orchestrator then independently found the full suite hanging catastrophically
(`npx vitest run --no-file-parallelism --exclude "e2e/**"`, this repo's standard verification
command) on two separate attempts, 16.7 minutes and 46 minutes respectively, each time on a
*different*, unrelated file (`MatrixPage.test.tsx` once, `RegistrationPage.test.tsx` the other
time — neither ever touched by this task), neither reproducing in isolation. This entry covers both
the original feature build (reviewed here, not previously written up) and the hang investigation.

**Part 1 — the feature (built by the prior session, reviewed and left unchanged by this one):**

- `frontend/src/lib/api/notifications.ts` — `fetchNotifications`/`markNotificationRead`/
  `markAllNotificationsRead` (→ P5-T06's `GET /notifications`, `POST /notifications/{id}/read`,
  `POST /notifications/read-all`), plus `useNotifications`/`useMarkNotificationRead`/
  `useMarkAllNotificationsRead`. Lives beside `lib/api/reference.ts` (the other non-surface-owned
  API module) rather than under any one `surfaces/*/api/`, since notifications are cross-cutting —
  every authenticated user has one inbox, visible from every surface.
- **Polling, not push:** `useNotifications` sets `refetchInterval: 60_000` — a real 60s poll. This
  is correct, deliberate product behavior (per the hook's own docstring, matching
  `api/routers/notifications.py`'s module docstring: no SSE/push exists for this low-urgency,
  in-app-only feed) and this investigation left it completely untouched — see Part 2 for why the
  fix belongs entirely in test infrastructure, not here.
- **No `AccessNotice` gate, and this is correct, not an oversight:** every other cross-surface
  addition in this codebase (`DownloadButton`, P5-T08) sits behind a `denied ? <AccessNotice/> :
  ...` branch because its endpoint requires a per-surface `Surface`/`Action` RBAC permission.
  `GET /notifications` et al. are gated on `get_current_principal` only (per P5-T06's own MEMORY.md
  entry and the router's module docstring) — every authenticated user, including a role that reads
  no surface at all, is entitled to read/manage their own inbox. An empty list for such a user is
  the correct "nothing to show you" outcome, not a permissions error, so `NotificationBell` never
  renders a denial state — confirmed by reading the component directly.
- **Mount point:** once, unconditionally, in `AppHeader` (`components/layout/app-header.tsx`) — the
  only cross-cutting chrome shared by all six surfaces — so the badge/list is reachable everywhere,
  not duplicated per-page. `NOTIFICATION_REASON_META` deliberately reuses `schedule-outcome-meta.ts`'s
  colour semantics (`delay_introduced`/`project_left_out` → warning, `conflict_raised` → danger) since
  these three reasons are directly downstream of the same P2 scheduling outcomes that module already
  covers — one colour vocabulary, not two, per the ui-ux-pro-max SKILL's colour+icon+label rule
  (verified: every badge in `NotificationRow` pairs tone with both an `Icon` and a text `label`).
  Single `useNotifications()` query drives both the header badge count and the dropdown list body
  (never a second "just the count" request), matching the backend's own always-present
  `unread_count` field design.
- No financial field ever appears in a notification message (confirmed: `NotificationRead.message`
  is server-composed from project/hub names and plain week numbers only, per P5-T06's backend).

**Part 2 — the full-suite hang: verification and fix.**

**Verified the hypothesis properly, did not just take it on faith.** The orchestrator's working
hypothesis was that `useNotifications()`'s real 60s `refetchInterval`, now mounted via
`AppHeader`/`NotificationBell` in every one of `app.test.tsx`'s `renderApp()` calls (10, not 9 —
recounted directly, an off-by-one in the orchestrator's own note, inconsequential either way), was
leaking real intervals past component unmount because TanStack Query's retry/refetch scheduling is
tied to the `Query` object in the cache, not the observer's React lifecycle. **Directly falsified
this specific claim** by patching `globalThis.setInterval`/`clearInterval` (temporary
instrumentation, removed before finishing) and running `app.test.tsx` alone: every `setInterval`
call at delay=60000 was matched 1:1 by a `clearInterval` call, net-pending count 0 after every one
of its 10 tests. Read `@tanstack/query-core`'s `queryObserver.js` directly to confirm why: v5's
`Observer.onUnsubscribe()` calls `destroy()` when the last listener detaches, which calls
`_clearRefetchInterval()` synchronously — RTL's `cleanup()` (wrapped in `act()`, called globally in
`src/test/setup.ts`) does trigger this correctly. **The refetch interval itself was never the
leak.**

**What actually is a real, confirmed leak** (found via the same instrumentation technique, applied
more broadly): `@tanstack/query-core`'s own `timeoutManager.js` module docstring states outright —
*"@tanstack/query-core makes liberal use of timeouts to implement staleTime and gcTime... known to
have scalability issues with thousands of timeouts on the event loop."* Every query schedules a
real `setTimeout` for `gcTime` (this app's shared default is `300_000ms` — `lib/query-client.ts`)
the moment its last observer unmounts; only `QueryClient.clear()` (or an individual
`queryCache.remove()`) ever cancels it (confirmed by reading `Removable.js`/`queryCache.js`
directly: `Query.destroy()` → `clearGcTimeout()`; `QueryClient.clear()` → `queryCache.clear()` →
`remove()` on every cached query → `destroy()`). Nothing in this codebase ever called `.clear()` on
a `QueryClient` after a test — every `renderWithProviders`/`renderApp()` call (`src/test/render.tsx`)
builds a brand-new real client and simply abandons it once the test ends. RTL's `cleanup()` unmounts
the component tree, which is what *triggers* `scheduleGc()` in the first place, but does nothing to
the orphaned client/cache itself.

Confirmed the real magnitude directly (temporary instrumentation: wrapped `globalThis.setTimeout`/
`clearTimeout`, counted net-pending calls with `delay >= 100000` — i.e. gcTime-class — via a
per-file `afterAll` writing to a scratch log; all instrumentation removed before finishing):
- Structural precondition confirmed via `ps` during a live run: `--no-file-parallelism` runs all 88
  files sequentially inside **one single forked worker process** (`vitest/dist/workers/forks.js`),
  so real Node timers scheduled while processing file A genuinely do persist into file B, C, ... —
  the theory is structurally possible, not ruled out by per-file isolation.
- An unfixed full run left **~130** such timers still pending at the end (none of them fire during
  a normal ~90s run since 300s always exceeds total suite duration — they just accumulate,
  each retaining its whole `QueryClient`/`QueryCache`/cached-response object graph, un-collectable,
  for the rest of the run, until Vitest force-kills the worker process at the very end — confirmed
  separately that Vitest does *not* wait for a natural process exit: a `process.on('exit', ...)`
  diagnostic never fired even on a clean run, consistent with a forceful worker termination rather
  than a graceful one).
- This pattern **predates P5-T09** — 7 other pre-existing files (`lib/api/notifications.test.tsx`
  plus one `use-*.test.tsx` hook test per surface, all from P4) construct `QueryClient` directly for
  `renderHook`, with the exact same never-disposed pattern. P5-T09 did not invent this leak, but
  measurably worsened it: `NotificationBell` is now mounted in every one of `app.test.tsx`'s 10
  `renderApp()` calls — the single highest-QueryClient-churn file in the suite, which does not mock
  `@/lib/api/*` at all, so the notifications query, like every other query on whichever surface
  each test renders, fails against the global `Promise.reject` fetch stub and retries, adding one
  more gc-timer-scheduling query per render.
- This is the most plausible mechanism for the reported symptom specifically: real timer/heap-
  retention pressure compounding across the sequential run, invisible to any single file in
  isolation (each starts clean) and only becoming pathological — a GC pause or timer-heap-insertion
  slowdown long enough to stall whatever `waitFor`/`act` polling loop happens to be running —
  once enough has piled up, which is consistent with hitting a different, unrelated test every
  time. **Caveat, stated plainly:** across 5 full clean runs performed both before and after the
  fix below (this machine, today), the hang itself never reproduced live — the orchestrator's two
  reported hangs were not independently re-triggered. The mechanism above is real, measured, and
  the most plausible candidate (and TanStack's own docs corroborate it as a genuine, known
  scalability failure mode of exactly this shape), but it should be read as "the best-supported,
  directly-confirmed root cause found by instrumentation," not as a live-reproduced hang.

**Fix — test-infra only, `frontend/src/test/setup.ts`:** patches `QueryClient.prototype.mount`
(called once by every `QueryClientProvider` for the client it wraps, regardless of which file or
helper constructed that client) to track every `QueryClient` instance the process ever mounts in a
module-level `Set`, then calls `.clear()` on every tracked client — synchronously cancelling every
one of its queries' gc timeouts — inside the existing global `afterEach`, *after* `cleanup()`.

Two design decisions worth recording, both arrived at after a failed first attempt each:
1. **Patches the third-party `QueryClient` class directly in `setup.ts`, rather than having
   `setup.ts` import a shared cleanup helper from `src/test/render.tsx`.** First attempt did exactly
   that and broke `notification-bell.test.tsx` (8 of 11 tests failing, confirmed by running that
   file alone): `setup.ts` runs before *every* test file, so eagerly importing `render.tsx` (which
   imports `@/app/routes` → `AppHeader` → `@/lib/api/notifications`) caches the real, unmocked
   `@/lib/api/notifications` module before that test file's own hoisted
   `vi.mock('@/lib/api/notifications', ...)` could register — the component under test ended up
   calling the real `useNotifications` (hitting the always-rejecting global fetch stub) instead of
   the test's `vi.fn()` mock. Patching `QueryClient` (a third-party class with no per-file mock to
   collide with) sidesteps this entirely; `render.tsx` itself is untouched, byte-for-byte identical
   to before this task.
2. **`.clear()` runs after `cleanup()`, explicitly, in the same hook** — not left to `afterEach`
   registration-order guesswork. Unmounting is what unsubscribes each query's last observer and
   triggers `scheduleGc()` in the first place; clearing first just lets a fresh gc timer get
   scheduled moments later by the unmount that follows, undoing most of the point (measured: an
   ordering-unsafe version of this fix only got the count down to ~102, not ~64).

**Honest result, not oversold:** this fix gets the still-pending-gc-timer count from ~130 down to
~64 at the end of a full run — **not all the way to 0.** Traced the remainder (per-file, via the
same instrumentation): 49 of the 64 are in `app.test.tsx` alone, the rest scattered 1-2 at a time
across the same 7 pre-existing `use-*.test.tsx`/`notifications.test.tsx` hook tests named above.
This residual has a different, narrower cause than the main leak: async work (an in-flight
retry/fetch) still outstanding at the exact moment a given test's `afterEach` runs, which schedules
its own gc timer moments later — after that test's `.clear()` sweep already ran and forgot about
the client, since the tracked-clients `Set` is emptied every `afterEach`. Fixing this fully would
mean auditing/rewriting several pre-existing P4 hook tests to properly await all in-flight
query/mutation settling before their own `afterEach` — out of scope for this task (none of those
files were touched by P5-T09, and the residual, at ~64, is nowhere near the "thousands" TanStack's
own docs identify as the actual danger threshold). Flagging as a real, small, understood remainder
for a future task, not silently closing the loop early.

**Full verification performed, fresh, after the fix:**
- `npx tsc -b --noEmit` — clean, 0 errors.
- `npx eslint .` — 0 errors, 1 pre-existing warning (`project-list.tsx`'s TanStack Virtual
  React-Compiler-incompatibility warning, unrelated to this task, unchanged from every prior P5
  entry's baseline).
- `pnpm build` — bundle-budget **PASS, 143.4 KB gzip initial load** (256.6 KB headroom against the
  400 KB budget). Up from P5-T08's 130.4 KB baseline — expected and correct, not a regression:
  unlike `DownloadButton` (lazy, per-surface-chunk only), `NotificationBell`/
  `notification-reason-meta.ts` are mounted unconditionally in `AppHeader`, part of the app shell
  itself, so they genuinely belong in the initial chunk. Still comfortably within budget.
- `npx vitest run --no-file-parallelism --exclude "e2e/**"` run **5 times in a row, back to back**
  (per this task's own instruction not to trust a single clean run given the reported flakiness):
  **88 files passed / 391 tests passed, every single time**, durations 53s / 66s / 70s / 70s / 71s —
  all comfortably under the ~2 minute target, no hang, no flake, no stray process left behind after
  any run (`ps aux | grep vitest` checked clean before the first run and after the last).

**Files touched:** `frontend/src/test/setup.ts` (the fix — `QueryClient.prototype.mount` patch +
tracked-client `.clear()` in the global `afterEach`; all temporary diagnostic instrumentation used
during investigation removed before finishing). `frontend/src/test/render.tsx` — touched during
investigation (an intermediate, ultimately-reverted attempt), confirmed byte-for-byte identical to
its pre-task state in the final diff; not part of the shipped fix. No other application code
touched — `frontend/src/lib/api/notifications.ts`, `notification-bell.tsx`,
`notification-reason-meta.ts`, `app-header.tsx` are exactly as the prior session left them, reviewed
but not modified.

**Flags for the reviewer:**
1. The ~64-timer residual described above (concentrated in `app.test.tsx` and the 7 pre-existing
   hook test files) is real and understood but not eliminated — a legitimate small follow-up if a
   future full-suite hang is ever observed again despite this fix.
2. This task did not independently reproduce the orchestrator's reported hang (5/5 clean runs). The
   fix is grounded in a real, measured, TanStack-Query-documented mechanism rather than a live

**2. Notification diff logic vs. `docs/DOMAIN_RULES.md` scheduling semantics — REAL MISMATCH FOUND,
BLOCKING.**

Read `backend/services/notifications.py` in full, then `backend/scheduling/greedy.py` and
`backend/scheduling/types.py` to independently re-derive what `end_week`/`within_year`/`spillover`
actually mean, per DOMAIN_RULES.md's "Completing within year" rule:
`!left_out AND (last_step_end + delay <= WITHIN_YEAR_WEEK)`.

- `greedy.py::_schedule_one_project` computes `end_week = steps_tuple[-1].end_week` — the **raw,
  undelayed** last-step finish week — then, **separately**, `completion_week = end_week +
  project.delay_weeks` (a local variable, never stored on `ProjectScheduleOutcome`) is what actually
  determines `within_year`/`spillover`. This is ADR 0004's documented, already-accepted "delay is a
  terminal adjustment, never a step-date shift" design (`docs/DOMAIN_RULES.md` known defect #3) —
  not itself something this review re-litigates.
- `Project.delay_weeks` is a real, user-editable field (`schemas/project.py`'s
  `ProjectUpdateRequest.delay_weeks`, `PUT /projects/{id}`) — the direct, ordinary way a planner
  records "this project slipped by N weeks."
- `services/notifications.py`'s `DELAY_INTRODUCED` trigger compares **only** `outcome.end_week`
  (new, in-memory) against `prev.last_step_end_week` (previous run's persisted
  `ScheduleRunProjectOutcome.last_step_end_week`) — both of which are the raw, undelayed figure.
  It never reads `within_year`, `spillover`, or `delay_weeks_applied` — all three of which are
  already computed by the scheduler and already persisted per-run on `ScheduleRunProjectOutcome`
  specifically so Invariant I9's Dashboard within-year count has a single source of truth.
- **Consequence, live-reproduced** (ephemeral test, `backend/tests/test_delay_gap_scratch.py`,
  written, run, and deleted during this review — not left in the repo): built a previous activated
  run's outcome (`left_out=False`, `last_step_end_week=40`) and a new run's in-memory outcome with
  the identical `end_week=40` but `within_year` flipped from `True` to `False`
  (`spillover=True`) — exactly what a `delay_weeks` increase produces, since delay_weeks is
  guaranteed by ADR 0004 to never move `end_week`. Called
  `generate_schedule_change_notifications` directly: **result `[]` — zero notifications**, for
  every eligible recipient, for a project that just became SPILLOVER.
- This is the single most common, most direct real-world "delay" scenario in the entire app (a
  planner records a schedule slip, re-runs and activates the schedule, the project's completion
  status genuinely worsens per DOMAIN_RULES.md's own rule) and it is completely invisible to the
  feature whose stated purpose (`docs/PROJECT_AND_STACK.md` §2, quoted in the module's own
  docstring) is exactly to surface "delay introduced... affecting a user's hub/projects." The
  module's chosen proxy for "delay" (`end_week` movement) excludes the domain's own named `delay`
  concept and the SPILLOVER completion rule entirely — a genuine inconsistency between the
  notification module's assumptions and the scheduler's actual semantics, which is precisely what
  this role's P5 checklist calls out as a real finding, not a style note.
- **Not a false alarm**: confirmed no other code path fires a notification for this transition —
  `PROJECT_LEFT_OUT` requires a `left_out` flip (not applicable, `left_out` is independent of
  `delay_weeks`), `CONFLICT_RAISED` is unrelated. Confirmed no existing test in
  `tests/test_notification_generation.py` covers this scenario (grepped every `def test_` in that
  file — none construct a same-`end_week`-different-`within_year` pair).
- **Recommended fix** (not actioned by this role, per the Delegation Rule): add a fourth condition
  to `generate_schedule_change_notifications` — `prev.within_year and not outcome.within_year` (a
  spillover transition independent of `end_week` movement) — either folded into `DELAY_INTRODUCED`
  or as its own reason, reusing the already-persisted `ScheduleRunProjectOutcome.within_year` field
  rather than re-deriving anything. This is a small, well-scoped fix (the persisted field already
  exists; the diff function already has both runs' outcome rows in scope).

**3. Invariant I9 posture on the three new P5 surfaces — PASS, verified by direct code read.**

  (`analytics_projects`/`hub_load_vs_capacity`/`list_priority_matrix`/`get_gantt`/`list_projects`/

- **New finding**: `ScenarioApplyRunSummary.change_count` (shown in the Versions & History list) is
  `services/scenario_apply.py`'s raw, portfolio-wide `len(changes)` computed once at Apply time —

  identical version. Both numbers are genuinely server-computed (no client-side recompute — I9 is

  the same class of problem (two views of one schedule-adjacent entity silently disagreeing) I9
  exists to prevent, just manifesting as a cross-endpoint backend inconsistency rather than a
  frontend one. **Not gate-blocking on its own** (lower real-world impact than finding #2 — it's a
  confusing count, not a missed alert — and the detail view's own empty-state already partially

  scope" qualifier in both views.

**5. Scenario-apply versioning vs. live `PriorityScore` — PASS, verified by direct code read.**

- `services/audit_helpers.py::priority_score_audit_state` and `api/routers/priorities.py::_build_row`

### [2026-09-05] P5 PHASE GATE: FAIL — rpd-orchestrator

Ran the P5 phase gate per this phase's own `docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` header ("Gate: qa-inspector
PASS + workflow-auditor PASS" — matching the P4 gate's established precedent of not requiring
security-auditor for a phase whose own header doesn't call for it; security gets its dedicated full
pass in P6-T07). All 9 P5 tasks (P5-T01 through P5-T09) were confirmed DONE before invoking the gate.

**qa-inspector: PASS.** Full detail in "[2026-09-05] P5 gate — qa-inspector" above — live re-run of
the entire backend (411/0/90.59%) and frontend (391/88, 3x back-to-back, no hangs) suites, contract
test confirmed still fixed, RBAC/financial-field/hub-scoping spot-checks against source. Two
non-blocking flags: no e2e/Playwright coverage for P5's four new UI features, and the documented
~64-timer test-infra residual (unchanged, not re-instrumented).

**workflow-auditor: FAIL.** Full detail in "[2026-09-05] P5 gate — workflow-auditor" above. Real,
live-reproduced domain-logic bug in `backend/services/notifications.py`'s `DELAY_INTRODUCED`
trigger: it compares raw `outcome.end_week`/`ScheduleRunProjectOutcome.last_step_end_week`, neither
of which ever includes `Project.delay_weeks` (confirmed independently: `scheduling/greedy.py`'s
`completion_week = end_week + project.delay_weeks` is computed and used only for the in-memory
`within_year`/`spillover` classification, never persisted as its own column;
`schedule_persistence.py:358` persists `last_step_end_week=outcome.end_week` — the undelayed value).
A planner recording a delay via `PUT /projects/{id}` (`delay_weeks`) — the single most direct,
ordinary real-world path to "this project is now delayed" in the whole app — can flip a project's
`within_year` from `True` to `False` (a genuine SPILLOVER regression) while `end_week` stays
identical, producing **zero notifications** for the exact condition the feature exists to catch.
Independently confirmed by reading `services/schedule_persistence.py`, `models/schedule.py`
(`within_year: Mapped[bool]` is itself already a persisted column on the same row —a more direct,
already-correct signal `notifications.py` doesn't use at all), and `scheduling/greedy.py` directly —
not just trusting workflow-auditor's writeup. A second, non-blocking finding was also flagged:
`ScenarioApplyRunSummary.change_count` (portfolio-wide, unfiltered) can silently disagree with the
same version's `ScenarioApplyRunDetail.changes` count (hub-scope-filtered per viewer) with no UI
indication the two counts differ in scope — real, but explicitly scoped by workflow-auditor as
follow-up, not independently gate-blocking.

**Verdict: P5 PHASE GATE FAILS.** Per CLAUDE.md's Gate Protocol, any one of the three required
agents has independent authority to FAIL regardless of the others' verdicts — qa-inspector's PASS
does not offset workflow-auditor's FAIL. P5 does not advance to P6 until the `DELAY_INTRODUCED`
defect is fixed (or explicitly superseded by an ADR narrowing the feature's scope, if the project
owner decides raw-end-week-only delay detection is an acceptable v1 limitation) and re-verified.
A remediation task (**P5-T10**) has been added at the top of the P5 task list in
`docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md`, per the Gate Protocol's "creates a remediation task at the top of the
current phase" instruction. The secondary version-history count-scope finding is recorded as a
follow-up note on that same task rather than a separate one, since both are most naturally fixed by

completion past the within-year cutoff" instead of the old "moved from week X to week Y" phrasing,

  — one image, three `command:`s, guaranteeing no code drift between what each container runs.
  `solver-worker` gets `mem_limit: 4g`, `mem_reservation: 1g`, `cpus: 2.0` (plain Compose-spec
  top-level keys, NOT `deploy.resources.limits` — verified live, see below, that plain
  `docker compose up` actually applies these to the container's `HostConfig`; `deploy.resources` is
  the Swarm-only path and was deliberately not used).
- `backend/Dockerfile` — multi-stage (`builder` with a C toolchain + venv, `runtime` slim
  `python:3.13-slim` with only the venv + app source, non-root `appuser`, `curl`-based
  `HEALTHCHECK` against `/healthz`). No dev/test dependencies shipped (`pip install .`, not
  `.[dev]`). Shared by `api`, `worker`, `solver-worker` — only `command:` differs per
  `docker-compose.yml`.
- `backend/docker-entrypoint.sh` — runs `alembic upgrade head` then `exec "$@"`. Applies to all
  three backend-image containers (idempotent no-op if already migrated); ensures a fresh
  `docker compose up` always has a current schema with no separate manual migration step.
- `backend/.dockerignore` — excludes `.venv/`, caches, `tests/`, `.env*` from the build context.
- `frontend/Dockerfile` — multi-stage (`node:20-alpine` + Corepack-pinned `pnpm@9` builder running
  `pnpm run build:no-budget`, then a bare `nginx:1.27-alpine` runtime serving only `dist/`). Decision
  (§6 offered a choice, "served by nginx or a small static service"): frontend is its OWN
  Compose service/container (a dedicated small nginx-static-file image), separate from the
  reverse-proxy `nginx` service — required by the acceptance criteria's own count ("all 8 services
  from the topology diagram" only totals 8 if `frontend` and `nginx` are distinct). `VITE_API_BASE_URL`
  is a build ARG defaulting to `/api` (baked into the JS bundle at build time, per Vite convention —
  verified present as a literal string in the built bundle) — chosen to reuse this repo's *existing*
  `vite.config.ts` dev/E2E proxy convention (`/api/*` -> backend, prefix stripped) rather than
  inventing a new one, since API routers mount at bare paths (`/projects`, `/healthz`, no `/api`
  prefix of their own — confirmed by reading `api/routers/projects.py`).
- `frontend/nginx.conf` — the static-file-serving container's own nginx config: SPA fallback
  (`try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html`, required for react-router client-side routes to survive a hard
  refresh) plus long-lived caching for content-hashed asset files only (never `index.html`).
- `frontend/.dockerignore` — excludes `node_modules`, `dist*`, `coverage`, Playwright artefacts,
  `.env*`.
- `deploy/nginx/default.conf` — the top-level reverse-proxy `nginx` service's config: `/api/` ->
  `api:8000/` (prefix stripped, `proxy_buffering off` + a 3600s read timeout for the solver-progress
  SSE stream), `/healthz` -> `api:8000/healthz` direct, `/` -> `frontend:80/`. Bare HTTP — TLS/HSTS/
  ModSecurity/OWASP CRS explicitly left for P6-T02, per this task's own "leave clean seams"
  instruction.
- `.env.example` (repo root) — every env var `docker-compose.yml` references
  (`POSTGRES_*`, `RPD_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `RPD_OIDC_*`, `RPD_MINIO_*`, optional
  `RPD_CELERY_*`, `HTTP_PORT`), placeholders only. Kept separate from (not merged into)
  `backend/.env.example`/`frontend/.env.example` — those remain the "run directly on a dev machine,
  outside Docker" templates; this new one is the Compose-stack template, reusing the exact same
  `RPD_*` variable names both already established.
- `.gitignore` (repo root — did not previously exist) — excludes `.env`/`.env.*` (keeping
  `*.env.example` tracked), matching the "no secrets in the repo" non-negotiable now that a root-level
  `.env` is a real artifact of this stack.

**Files edited (small, in-scope, non-scheduling backend fixes needed for the acceptance criteria to
actually be true, not just written):**
- `backend/pyproject.toml` — removed `readme = false`. This is not a valid PEP 621 value (must be a
  string, a table, or omitted); modern `setuptools`/`validate-pyproject` (as pulled into the
  `python:3.13-slim` build image) rejects it outright, which is why `docker build` failed on first
  attempt (real bug caught live, not assumed) with `ValueError: invalid pyproject.toml config:
  project.readme`. This never surfaced locally because the dev `.venv` had never actually run
  `pip install .` against this file. Fixed by omitting the field entirely (same net effect: no
  readme declared).
- `backend/workers/celery_app.py` / `backend/workers/worker_app.py` — added
  `task_default_queue="solver"` / `task_default_queue="worker"` respectively. Celery's actual default
  queue name is the literal string `"celery"` regardless of the `Celery(main, ...)` app name — without
  this, BOTH apps' tasks would publish to that same default queue despite sharing one Redis broker
  (`docs/PROJECT_AND_STACK.md` §6's single-Redis topology), which would either mean `worker_app.py`'s
  own documented `--queues=worker` startup flag (already in its docstring, pre-existing) silently
  never received any tasks, or — if that flag were dropped — `worker` and `solver-worker` cross-
  subscribing to each other's tasks (`NotRegistered` errors), quietly undoing the "solver-worker...
  isolated for resource limits" design both files' own docstrings already promised. This is the
  concrete fix that makes the P6-T01 acceptance criterion "worker and solver-worker are genuinely
  separate containers/processes... run different Celery queue names" literally true rather than
  cosmetic. Verified live (see below): `worker`'s log banner shows `[queues] .> worker` /
  `[tasks] . workers.generate_export`; `solver-worker`'s shows `[queues] .> solver` /
  `[tasks] . workers.run_cp_sat_schedule`. No existing test asserted the old (queue-name-unset)
  behavior — `backend/tests/test_workers_celery_app.py` re-run clean, full suite re-run clean
  (415 passed, 89.67% coverage; `backend/scheduling/`'s own 85% gate suite also re-run clean, 80
  passed, 93.58% coverage — that package was not touched).
- `Makefile` — added `dev` (`docker compose up -d --build`), `dev-down`, `dev-logs` targets; updated

**Deviations from a literal reading of §6:**
- Frontend is served by its OWN nginx container (a "small static service" in §6's own wording, just
  implemented as nginx-serving-static rather than e.g. a Node/Caddy static server), kept separate
  from the top-level reverse-proxy `nginx` service, rather than baking the built assets directly into
  the edge nginx container. Rationale: matches the acceptance criteria's explicit 8-service count and
  keeps a frontend-only redeploy from ever touching the P6-T02-owned edge/TLS container.
- Production routing convention is `/api/*` (prefix stripped) for the backend, `/` for the frontend
  SPA — not literally specified in §6, but required because API routers and the frontend both use
  bare/overlapping path namespaces (e.g. a future `/projects` frontend route vs. the existing
  `/projects` API router) at the same origin; this reuses `vite.config.ts`'s own pre-existing dev/E2E
  proxy convention rather than inventing a new one.
- `mem_limit`/`cpus` (plain Compose-spec keys) chosen over `deploy.resources.limits` for
  `solver-worker`, specifically because the latter is not reliably honored by plain `docker compose
  up` outside Swarm — confirmed by direct experiment, not just documentation-reading (see point 5
  above).
- `api`'s entrypoint runs `alembic upgrade head` before starting Gunicorn (not specified in §6, which
  is silent on migration timing) — chosen so a fresh `docker compose up` never requires a separate
  manual migration step; `worker`/`solver-worker` inherit the same entrypoint (harmless/idempotent
  re-run) rather than adding an `entrypoint: []` override, so either one starting independently of
  `api` (e.g. a partial restart) still guarantees a current schema.
- `RPD_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY`/`RPD_MINIO_SECRET_KEY` double as MinIO's own `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/
  `MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` (one credential pair, not two) — not specified either way in §6.
- MinIO's own web console/API port is not published to the host (internal-only — exports are
  downloaded via the `api` service, the browser never talks to MinIO directly) — a deliberate
  security-minded default, commented out and easy to re-enable per-deployment if an operator wants
  direct console access.

### [2026-09-05] P6-T02 — backend-builder: TLS 1.3, HSTS, ModSecurity + OWASP CRS at the edge reverse proxy

**Did:** Hardened the internet-facing edge `nginx` service from P6-T01 (`deploy/nginx/default.conf`
+ `docker-compose.yml`) with TLS termination, HSTS + baseline security headers, and a real
ModSecurity + OWASP CRS WAF hop in front of both `/api/*` and `/` traffic. `frontend/nginx.conf`
(internal-only, per P6-T01) was NOT touched, per that task's own note.

**Architecture decision (not a literal single-file edit):** rather than hand-building a custom
ModSecurity-nginx image or trying to reverse-engineer the official `owasp/modsecurity-crs` image's
envsubst-templated single-`BACKEND` config to route two upstreams from one container, this task adds
**two new dedicated WAF containers**, `waf-api` and `waf-frontend` (`docker-compose.yml`), each
running the official image in its default one-`BACKEND` reverse-proxy mode, pointed at `api:8000`
and `frontend:80` respectively. The edge `nginx` (`deploy/nginx/default.conf`) keeps doing exactly
what P6-T01 built (TLS/headers/routing/SSE-buffering) but now proxies `/api/` to `waf-api:8080` and
`/` to `waf-frontend:8080` instead of straight to `api`/`frontend`. Neither WAF container is
published to the host — only `nginx` is, on both 80 and 443, preserving P6-T01's "nginx is the ONLY
container that publishes a port" invariant. `/healthz` deliberately bypasses the WAF hop entirely
(routed straight to `api:8000/healthz`) — it's an orchestration liveness probe with no user input,
not part of the WAF-guarded surface, and this keeps the healthcheck meaningful (real `api` health,
not a synthetic "OK" from the WAF image's own stub `/healthz` location).

**Files created:**
- `deploy/tls/generate-dev-cert.sh` — idempotent DEV-ONLY self-signed cert/key generator
  (`deploy/tls/dev/{server.crt,server.key}`, gitignored), clearly commented as never the production
  artifact. Wired into `make dev` as a new `dev-tls-cert` prerequisite target (`Makefile`).

**Files edited:**
- `docker-compose.yml` — added `x-waf-image`/`x-waf-common-env` YAML anchors, two new services
  (`waf-frontend`: stock CRS defaults, only serves static GETs; `waf-api`: three narrowly-scoped
  tuning overrides, see below), and edited the `nginx` service: publishes 443 alongside 80, mounts
  `RPD_TLS_CERT_PATH`/`RPD_TLS_KEY_PATH` (both `${VAR:?err}`-guarded, same convention as every other
  required secret in this file) to fixed in-container paths, `depends_on` now includes
  `waf-api`/`waf-frontend`, and the healthcheck now hits an internal-only `:8080` listener instead of
  `:80` (see below for why).
- `deploy/nginx/default.conf` — full rewrite: HTTP (80) is now redirect-only (never serves content,
  per the acceptance criteria's literal wording); a new internal-only `:8080` server block exists
  solely so the container's own Docker `HEALTHCHECK` can probe liveness in plain HTTP (`nginx:1.27-
  alpine`'s busybox `wget` has no `--no-check-certificate`-equivalent flag — confirmed via `wget
  --help` inside the image — so probing HTTPS directly from inside the container wasn't viable; this
  port is never published to the host, so it doesn't weaken "port 80 only redirects" in any way a
  real client could exploit); the real HTTPS (443) server block does TLS termination + HSTS +
  baseline headers + the same `/healthz` (direct-to-`api`, bypasses WAF) / `/api/` (now ->
  `waf-api`) / `/` (now -> `waf-frontend`) routing P6-T01 built, unchanged otherwise (SSE
  buffering/timeout settings on `/api/` carried forward verbatim).
- `.env.example` — added `HTTPS_PORT`, `RPD_TLS_CERT_PATH`, `RPD_TLS_KEY_PATH` (defaults point at the
  dev-generated self-signed pair, loudly commented "REPLACE THESE TWO PATHS before any real
  deployment").
- `.gitignore` — added `deploy/tls/dev/` (the generated dev cert material; the generator script
  itself stays tracked).
- `Makefile` — `dev` now depends on a new `dev-tls-cert` target (idempotent, runs the generator
  script).

**TLS decision:** `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;` — both enabled (TLS 1.3 always wins the handshake
against any client that supports it; there's no separate "prefer" directive beyond listing it). TLS
1.2 kept, not disabled, for compatibility with any older internal tooling/monitoring on Frigoglass's
corporate network (on-premise deployment, not a public site with an assumed-modern client
population) — mirrors Mozilla's "Intermediate" TLS profile. TLS 1.0/1.1/SSLv3 never offered (not in
the allow-list). Cipher list is Mozilla Intermediate's AEAD/ECDHE-only set for the TLS 1.2 leg (TLS
1.3's own suite set isn't configurable via `ssl_ciphers`); `ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off` per current
Mozilla guidance since every offered cipher is already strong.

**HSTS decision:** `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` — NO `preload`. Preload is designed for
public-internet domains submitted to browser-shipped preload lists; this is an on-premise app behind
Frigoglass's corporate network with no public DNS presence to preload, and preload submission is
effectively hard-to-reverse. `includeSubDomains` without `preload` already gives strong protection
for this deployment shape.

**CSP decision:** no CSP existed anywhere in the repo before this task (checked `frontend/index.html`
and all of `frontend/src` — no meta-tag CSP, no header-setting code, no CDN/external-font/script
references at all — everything is same-origin). Added a new, deliberately minimal baseline at the
edge: `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self';
frame-ancestors 'self'; upgrade-insecure-requests`. `'unsafe-inline'` on `script-src`/`style-src` is a
known, flagged gap (not a full audit — that's P6-T07's job per this task's own scope note):
`frontend/index.html` has a small inline `<script>` for the pre-first-paint theme flash fix, and
Framer Motion/Tailwind's runtime styling behavior wasn't fully audited for inline `style` attribute
usage. Flagged for P6-T07 to tighten to a nonce- or hash-based policy.

**ModSecurity/CRS decisions:**
- Image: `owasp/modsecurity-crs:4.28.0-nginx-alpine-202608131208` — the official, actively maintained
  image (checked Docker Hub tag list live; CRS 4.28.0 is the current latest stable release family as
  of this task). Pinned to a specific dated stable-tag build, not the floating `nginx-alpine` rolling
  tag (the image's own README explicitly advises against rolling tags in production). Re-pin/digest
  discipline going forward is P6-T05's job, per the same precedent P6-T01 set for `minio:latest`.
- `BLOCKING_PARANOIA=1` (the image default) on both WAF instances, left deliberately unraised. CRS's
  own guidance is to start production at PL1 (lowest false-positive rate) and only raise it after a
  monitoring period against real traffic. This app has free-text fields (scenario `notes`,
  priority-score justification text) that are exactly the kind of input PL2+'s more aggressive
  generic-attack heuristics tend to false-positive on — raising it is a P6-T07/ops decision made
  after observing real audit-log data, not a one-shot guess made here.
- Three narrowly-scoped overrides on `waf-api` only (checked `backend/api/routers/*.py` and
  `backend/schemas/scenario.py` directly, per the task's own instruction, rather than guessing):
  `ALLOWED_METHODS` extended to include PUT/PATCH/DELETE (the API genuinely uses all five verbs —
  `grep -rhoE '@router\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)' backend/api/routers/*.py` counted 37/11/3/2/2;
  the image's stock default is a static-site-shaped "GET HEAD POST OPTIONS", which would 403 every
  real PUT/PATCH/DELETE call via CRS's own method-allowlist rule 911100); `MODSEC_REQ_BODY_NOFILES_
  LIMIT` raised 128 KiB -> 5 MiB and `MODSEC_ARGUMENTS_LIMIT` raised 1000 -> 10000, both because `POST
  /scenarios/apply`'s `ScenarioApplyRequest.priority_scores` is a genuine bulk-edit array that can
  span every active project's every priority dimension at once (~236 projects x 13 dimensions per
  DOMAIN_RULES.md) — comfortably past both defaults as JSON, which would otherwise trip ModSecurity's
  own body-size rejection and CRS's `REQBODY_ERROR`-driven rule 200002. `waf-frontend` keeps every CRS
  tuning variable at the image default (static GET/HEAD/OPTIONS traffic only, none of the above
  applies).

**Live verification performed (real `docker compose up -d --build`, full 10-service stack, torn down
+ `.env`/dev-cert cleaned up after):**
1. `docker compose config --quiet` — exit 0.
2. `docker compose up -d --build` — all 10 containers (8 from P6-T01 + `waf-api`/`waf-frontend`)
   started; all healthchecks (including the new `nginx` `:8080`-based one) reached `healthy`.
3. TLS 1.3: `echo | openssl s_client -connect localhost:8443 -tls1_3` -> `Protocol: TLSv1.3, Cipher:
   TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`; `curl -sk -v https://127.0.0.1:8443/healthz` (host curl, SecureTransport
   backend) independently confirmed `SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / AEAD-CHACHA20-POLY1305-SHA256`
   plus `using HTTP/2`. TLS 1.2: `openssl s_client -tls1_2` -> `Protocol: TLSv1.2, Cipher: ECDHE-RSA-
   AES256-GCM-SHA384`. TLS 1.0/1.1 client attempts failed locally before reaching the server (the
   local OpenSSL build itself refuses to offer those protocols) — not a server-side proof, but
   `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;` is an allow-list directive, so anything not listed is structurally
   unreachable by config, not by chance.
4. HTTP->HTTPS redirect: `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} -> %{redirect_url}' http://localhost:8080/anything`
   -> `301 -> https://localhost/anything` (no body served).
5. Headers on a real HTTPS response (`curl -sk -D - https://localhost:8443/healthz`): `strict-
   transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`, `x-content-type-options: nosniff`,
   `x-frame-options: DENY`, `referrer-policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, and the full CSP
   string above — all present, and independently confirmed still present on a WAF-blocked 403
   response too (headers survive a block, not just a 200).
6. WAF block test: `GET /api/projects?id=1%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271` (URL-encoded classic SQLi) via
   the real edge on 8443 -> **403** (CRS-generated Forbidden page). A second XSS-shaped query
   (`<script>alert(1)</script>`) -> **403**. A SQLi string embedded inside a legitimate-shaped JSON
   POST body to `/api/scenarios/apply` -> **403** — confirms the body-size/argument-count/method
   overrides above did not disable real attack detection.
7. Legitimate pass-through: unauthenticated `GET /api/projects` -> **401** `{"detail":"Missing
   Authorization header"}` (real FastAPI response, not a WAF block); `GET /api/docs` and `GET
   /api/openapi.json` -> **200**; `GET /` (frontend) -> **200**; unauthenticated `PUT
   /api/currency-rates/EUR` -> **401** (proves the `ALLOWED_METHODS` override works — PUT reaches the
   app instead of being 403'd by CRS); unauthenticated `POST /api/scenarios/apply` with a real
   306 KB / 3000-entry synthetic bulk `priority_scores` array -> **401** (proves the raised body-
   size/argument-count overrides work — the request reached the app, not blocked at the WAF).
8. **Differential proof the overrides were load-bearing, not cosmetic:** spun up a throwaway third
   `owasp/modsecurity-crs` container on the same network with the image's stock (unmodified) defaults
   and `BACKEND=http://api:8000`, then sent the identical 306 KB bulk-JSON body and PUT request
   directly to it (bypassing the edge, to isolate the WAF layer): the 306 KB body -> **400** (rejected
   by the default body/argument limits) and the PUT -> **403** (rejected by the default
   `ALLOWED_METHODS`) — both exactly the false positives predicted, confirming the `waf-api`-specific
   overrides in `docker-compose.yml` are the actual fix, not a redundant no-op.
9. `docker compose down -v` — clean teardown; throwaway `.env` and generated dev cert both removed

### [2026-09-05] P6-T04 — backend-builder: Docker Compose secrets wiring; confirm zero secrets in repo history

**Did:** Moved every genuinely sensitive value the P6-T01/T02 compose stack was passing as plain
`environment:` interpolation — Postgres password, `RPD_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, MinIO access/secret
key pair — into Docker Compose's native `secrets:` construct (files under `./secrets/`, mounted
read-only at `/run/secrets/<name>`), and prepared (but did not activate — P6-T03 is BLOCKED) an
identical slot for a future OIDC confidential-client secret. Confirmed the repo tree has zero real
secrets anywhere a `git init` could pick them up (there is still no `.git` — confirmed again before
starting).

**Decision — Docker Compose secrets, not Vault:** this is a single-client, on-premise Compose
deployment (not Kubernetes) with no existing Vault install and no dynamic-secret-leasing or
multi-tenant requirement that would justify Vault's unseal/init/policy-management operational
burden. Compose's native `secrets:` gets the two things that matter here — secret material off
`docker inspect`'s `Config.Env` / `/proc/<pid>/environ` / shell history, and out of `.env` files —
with zero extra infrastructure, consistent with the "clean seams, no unrequested infra" precedent
P6-T01/T02 already set. Full reasoning in `secrets/README.md`'s own "Why Docker Compose secrets and
not Vault" section.

**Mechanism chosen:** rather than requiring every consumption site to learn a new convention, this
task adds ONE generic `_FILE`-suffix resolution shim (`resolve_secret()` in
`backend/docker-entrypoint.sh`, POSIX `sh`/dash-compatible) that runs before `alembic upgrade head`
and before any Python starts, for ALL THREE backend containers (`api`/`worker`/`solver-worker` — all
three share this entrypoint; confirmed live via container logs, not assumed). It reads
`<NAME>_FILE` env vars (Compose-set to `/run/secrets/<secret>` paths) and exports the resolved value
into the plain `<NAME>` env var this codebase's existing config-loading code already reads —
`os.environ.get("RPD_DATABASE_URL"/"RPD_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY")` in `backend/api/db.py`,
`backend/alembic/env.py`, `backend/workers/*.py`, `backend/models/types.py`, and `pydantic-settings`
`BaseSettings` subclasses (`MinioSettings` in `backend/core/minio_config.py`, which reads
`os.environ` the same way) for `RPD_MINIO_*`. **Zero Python code changes were needed** — this was
the deciding factor over inventing a custom pydantic-settings secrets source, since the codebase
already has three different consumption conventions (plain `os.environ.get`, `pydantic-settings`
`BaseSettings`, and Alembic's own `env.py`) and a shell-level shim is the only mechanism that covers
all three uniformly without touching any of them.
`RPD_DATABASE_URL` specifically can't be Compose-interpolated from a secret (compose-level `${VAR}`
interpolation only sees host/`.env` values, never file-mounted secrets) — so it is now assembled
*inside* the shim from non-secret `POSTGRES_USER`/`POSTGRES_DB`/`POSTGRES_HOST`/`POSTGRES_PORT`
(plain config) plus the resolved `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` secret, exported before `alembic upgrade head`
runs. `postgres` and `minio`'s own containers use their **native** `_FILE` support instead of the
custom shim (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE` is docker-library's own `file_env` convention; `MINIO_ROOT_
USER_FILE`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD_FILE` confirmed present via `strings` on the actual pulled
`minio/minio:latest` binary — not assumed from memory of old docs).

**Files created:**
- `secrets/.gitkeep`, `secrets/README.md` — the only two tracked files under `secrets/`; README
  documents the config-vs-secret line this app draws (table), what to generate and how (`openssl
  rand`, Fernet-key one-liner), the future OIDC-client-secret slot, and the Vault-vs-Docker-secrets
  rationale.
- `deploy/secrets/generate-dev-secrets.sh` — idempotent DEV-ONLY generator mirroring
  `deploy/tls/generate-dev-cert.sh`'s (P6-T02) own pattern exactly (never overwrites an existing
  file, wired into `make dev` as a new `dev-secrets` prerequisite). Generates the Fernet key via
  `openssl rand -base64 32 | tr '+/' '-_'` rather than assuming `python3`+`cryptography` exist on the
  HOST (only guaranteed inside the backend container/venv) — verified the output is a valid,
  loadable Fernet key (`Fernet(key.encode())` succeeds) before relying on it.

**Files edited:**
- `docker-compose.yml` — added a top-level `secrets:` map (4 entries); `x-backend-image` anchor's
  `environment:` block: removed `RPD_DATABASE_URL`/`RPD_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY`/`RPD_MINIO_ACCESS_KEY`/
  `RPD_MINIO_SECRET_KEY` as plain `${VAR:?err}` interpolation entirely; added `POSTGRES_USER`/
  `POSTGRES_DB`/`POSTGRES_HOST`/`POSTGRES_PORT` (config) plus the four `*_FILE` secret-path vars and
  a `secrets:` list; added a commented-out `RPD_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE` future slot with inline
  instructions for P6-T03. `postgres` service: `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` → `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE` +
  `secrets:` list (native image support). `minio` service: `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` →
  `MINIO_ROOT_USER_FILE`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD_FILE` + `secrets:` list (native image support,
  confirmed via binary `strings`, not docs alone). Updated the file's own top-of-file "Usage" comment

- `backend/docker-entrypoint.sh` — added the `resolve_secret()` shim (documented above) plus

**Config vs. secret — the line drawn (also in `secrets/README.md`):** config = hostnames, ports,
feature flags, OIDC issuer/audience/client-id (client-id is a public identifier, not a credential,
per `core/oidc.py`'s own docstring), TLS cert/key *paths* (the files themselves are already
file-mounted as of P6-T02, untouched by this task). Secret = Postgres password, the field-encryption
Fernet key, the MinIO access/secret key pair, and (future, P6-T03) an OIDC confidential-client
secret — anything that grants data access or lets someone decrypt/impersonate.

     layer (`msgpack`, `setuptools`). With `--ignore-unfixed` added: the 63 OS findings **all**
     disappeared (Debian has published no fix yet for any of them — confirmed by the flag alone
     zeroing them out) — this is the concrete, live-verified reason `--ignore-unfixed` is this task's
     chosen policy (see below), not a guess. The remaining 2 Python-layer HIGH findings were
     individually verified to be **Trivy false positives**: neither `msgpack` nor `setuptools` is
     actually present anywhere in the built image's `/opt/venv` (checked via `find` and
     `importlib.metadata` inside a running container of the actual image — `ModuleNotFoundError` for
     both). Root cause for `msgpack`: `kombu`'s own `METADATA` declares
     `Requires-Dist: msgpack==1.1.2; extra == "msgpack"`, an **optional, unrequested** extra
     (`celery[redis]` doesn't request `kombu[msgpack]`) that Trivy's Python-package parser
     misattributes as installed. `setuptools` similarly has no installed dist-info anywhere in the
     image. **Real, actionable baseline for `rpd-backend`: zero.**
   - **`rpd-frontend`** (from `frontend/Dockerfile`, `nginx:1.27-alpine` runtime base): with
     `--ignore-unfixed` + `CRITICAL,HIGH`: **34 real, actionable findings** (2 CRITICAL —

     `c-ares`, `musl`, `nghttp2`, `zlib`), all with fixed versions already published in Alpine's own
     package repo. Root cause confirmed live: `docker pull nginx:1.27-alpine` today still resolves to
     the same digest last pushed 2025-04-16 (`docker inspect` `.Created`) — the tag itself is stale,
     re-pulling doesn't help. **Fixed in this task** (see "Files edited" below) by adding
     `RUN apk update && apk upgrade --no-cache` to the runtime stage — verified via an isolated
     before/after rebuild-and-rescan (34 findings -> 0), confirmed same Alpine 3.21 release line (no
     major OS bump), same nginx version, and confirmed no behavior change (`nginx -t` passes inside
     the patched image; a live container of the patched image serves `/` -> `200` and `/dashboard`
     (SPA fallback) -> `200`). This is the one "trivially and safely upgradable with no behavior risk"
     change made per the task's own stated exception — not a lockfile/dependency-version change, so
     `make test`/Vitest were not re-run (nothing in `package.json`/`pnpm-lock.yaml` changed); the
     Docker-level verification above (build + `nginx -t` + live `curl` 200) is the actual applicable
     regression check for a Dockerfile-only change.
   - **Third-party pulled images (lighter pass, as the task invited "your call, document it"):**
     `redis:7-alpine` clean (0 with `--ignore-unfixed`); `postgres:17-alpine` 9 HIGH
     (`libcrypto3`/`libssl3`/`libuuid`, fixes available); `owasp/modsecurity-crs:4.28.0-nginx-alpine-202608131208`
     11 OS-package findings; `minio/minio:latest` the standout — dozens of HIGH + several CRITICAL
     (`CVE-2026-56854` `golang.org/x/crypto`, `CVE-2026-33186` `google.golang.org/grpc`,
     `CVE-2025-68121` Go stdlib, among many others) across its bundled `mc`/`minio` Go binaries — this
     is the live, concrete evidence behind P6-T01's own flag that `minio/minio:latest` "is
     intentionally left floating... flagging P6-T05 as where pin discipline belongs." **Not
     remediated in this task** — a version bump for a pulled infrastructure image needs a full
     compose-stack re-verification pass (MinIO API/config compatibility across versions), which is a
     remediation task of its own, not a scanning-wiring task; the CI job wired here (report-only,
     weekly/manual, non-blocking) surfaces these for that decision going forward instead of leaving
     them unmonitored indefinitely.

**Severity/failure policy chosen per scanner (documented inline in the workflow YAML too):**
- `pip-audit`: fail on **any** known vulnerability, no severity filter — PyPI/OSV advisories for
  Python packages carry no uniform CVSS severity the way Trivy's OS/container advisories do, and the
  `security-review` skill states this scanner's bar as "on every backend dependency change" with no
  stated tolerance. Escape hatch for a genuinely unfixable low-risk finding (the precedent already set
  once by the ecdsa case): an explicit `--ignore-vuln <ID>` added to the workflow with a comment citing
  the `docs/MEMORY.md` finding and a review date — never silent, never blanket.
- `pnpm audit`: `--audit-level=high` — fails only on High/Critical. Verified live that this exits `0`
  today (the 2 real findings are both Moderate) while still printing them in the job log. Chosen
  because this frontend's dependency tree is large enough that gating every PR on every transitive
  Low/Moderate advisory would make the check permanently red and get ignored — not a usable gate,
  per the task's own explicit warning against that failure mode.
- Trivy (owned images, `rpd-backend`/`rpd-frontend`): `--severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed`,
  blocking (`exit-code: 1`) on every push/PR. `--ignore-unfixed` is not a weakening of the gate — it's
  what makes the gate usable at all, live-proven above (63 permanently-unfixed OS findings on the
  backend image's Debian-trixie base alone would otherwise make this job permanently red with zero
  remediation path). Real, fixable findings (the frontend's 34) DO fail the gate and DID get fixed.
- Trivy (third-party pulled images): same severity filter, but **report-only**
  (`exit-code: 0`, weekly/manual trigger only, never blocks push/PR) — this repo doesn't control these
  images' build process, so blocking every PR on an upstream base image's CVE isn't proportionate;
  surfaced periodically instead for a deliberate pin/upgrade decision.

**Files edited:**
- `frontend/Dockerfile` — added `RUN apk update && apk upgrade --no-cache` to the runtime stage
  (see Trivy findings above for the full before/after verification). This is the only dependency/
  image-level change made in this task.

### [2026-09-05] P6-T06 — backend-builder: Observability (structured logging, /metrics, backup/restore drill)

**Did:** Three parts, all live-verified against the real P6-T01/T02/T04 Docker Compose stack.

**Part 1 — structured (JSON) logging, no PII.**
- `backend/core/logging_config.py` (new): `JsonFormatter` (stdlib `logging`, hand-rolled — no
  `structlog`/`python-json-logger` dependency existed and none was needed), a `request_id_ctx`
  `ContextVar` for correlation, `LoggingSettings` (`RPD_LOG_*`, default `INFO`), and idempotent
  `configure_logging(service)` that replaces the root logger's handlers with one JSON stdout handler.
- `backend/core/observability.py` (new): `ObservabilityMiddleware` — a raw ASGI middleware
  (deliberately NOT `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, which is documented to risk breaking long-lived streaming
  responses; this app has a real one, `GET /schedule-runs/{id}/progress` SSE) that assigns/propagates
  a `request_id` (header + contextvar), times the request, and emits one structured
  `http_request_completed` log line per request with `http_method`/`http_route` (the ROUTE TEMPLATE,
  e.g. `/projects/{project_id}`, resolved from `scope["route"]` post-routing — never the raw path with
  a real id, and never the query string, which is never read by this middleware at all).
- `backend/gunicorn_conf.py` (new): routes Gunicorn's own access/error logs (and `uvicorn.access`/
  `uvicorn.error`, which `UvicornWorker` defers to Gunicorn's own logging config for) through the same
  `JsonFormatter`. `access_log_format` overridden to `%(U)s` (path only, never `%(r)s`'s full request
  line with query string) — defense-in-depth even though `grep -rn "Query(" api/routers/*.py` found
  zero query-param filters anywhere in this app today.
- `backend/core/celery_logging.py` (new): `install_celery_logging`/`install_task_duration_logging`,
  shared by `workers/celery_app.py` and `workers/worker_app.py` (both call these at import time).
  Wires Celery's `setup_logging` signal to `configure_logging` (stops Celery's own default
  plain-text logging setup) and `task_prerun`/`task_postrun` to emit one `task_completed` log line per
  finished task (`task_name`, `queue`, `state`, `duration_seconds` — never the task's own ARGUMENTS,
  since an export task's `filters` payload is not guaranteed PII-free even though this app's other
  task payloads happen to be just UUIDs). Real bug caught and fixed during this task: Celery's
  `task_prerun`/`task_postrun` signals are process-global, not scoped per `Celery` app instance — a
  test that imports both `workers.celery_app` and `workers.worker_app` in the same process (as this
  repo's test suite now does) double-logged every task once per installed app until both receiver
  bodies were changed to check `task.app is app` and skip otherwise. Harmless in production (each
  container only ever imports ONE of the two app modules — confirmed via
  `grep -rn "from workers\." backend/` — `solver-worker` never imports `workers.worker_app` and vice
  versa) but genuinely wrong before the fix for any process that imports both.
- `backend/workers/schedule_tasks.py`: added one structured log line after `run_cp_sat` returns
  (`solver_status`, `solve_wall_time_seconds`) — CP-SAT solve time is a reasonable, non-sensitive
  aggregate performance number per this task's own guidance, never tied to a named project/customer.
- `backend/api/main.py`: calls `configure_logging("api")` before any router import (several routers
  create a module-level `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` at import time) and
  `app.add_middleware(ObservabilityMiddleware)`.
- **PII/financial audit performed** (per CLAUDE.md's "never logged" non-negotiable and
  `docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` #8): read every existing `logging.`/`logger`/`print(` call site in
  `backend/api/`, `backend/services/`, `backend/workers/`, `backend/core/` before writing any new
  code (`grep -rn "logging\.\|logger\|print(" ...` across those four dirs). **Finding: zero fixes
  needed.** Every existing call site (`workers/export_tasks.py`, `workers/schedule_tasks.py`,
  `api/routers/schedule_runs.py`) already only logs opaque identifiers (job/run UUIDs, surface/format
  names, row counts, solver status/timing) — never a decrypted financial value, customer name, or
  engineer name. `services/audit_helpers.py` (a SEPARATE concern, the immutable append-only audit
  trail per `models/audit.py` — deliberately not touched or duplicated by this task, confirmed to
  already redact the four `FINANCIAL_FIELD_NAMES` unconditionally as `"<redacted>"` without ever
  calling the ORM attribute getter that would trigger decryption) was equally clean. `seed/*.py`
  scripts `print()` only row-count summaries. Standing line drawn for this task's own new code (also
  documented in `core/logging_config.py`'s module docstring): correlate by `request_id` (random,
  person-agnostic) — `docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` #8 is scoped to named-engineer utilization VIEWS/EXPORTS,
  not bare request correlation, so this is not the same concern.
- Live-verified with the real stack up (`docker compose up -d --build`, all 12 services incl. the new
  `beat`): `api`'s log stream is 100% JSON from Gunicorn boot through every access line (only the
  Celery ASCII-art startup banners and a handful of `alembic upgrade head` lines — a separate `alembic`
  CLI subprocess invocation predating Python logging setup, pre-existing since P6-T01, not fixed here
  as a marginal/non-PII cosmetic gap — are non-JSON); `worker`/`solver-worker`/`beat` are JSON after
  their own startup banners; a real request through nginx→WAF→api (`curl -sk https://localhost/api/healthz`)
  produced a matching `{"logger": "api.access", "message": "http_request_completed", "request_id": ...,
  "http_route": "/healthz", "http_status": 200, "duration_ms": ...}` line with no query string, no
  financial field, no name of any kind.

**Part 2 — metrics.**
- `backend/pyproject.toml`: added `prometheus-client>=0.21` (no such dependency existed before;
  checked first). Deliberately not `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator` (same
  `BaseHTTPMiddleware`/SSE-streaming risk as above).
- `GET /metrics` (`api/main.py`, backed by `core/observability.py::render_metrics`): Prometheus
  text-exposition format, unauthenticated (same posture as `/healthz`), `rpd_http_requests_total`
  (Counter, labels `method`/`route`/`status`) and `rpd_http_request_duration_seconds` (Histogram,
  labels `method`/`route`) — bounded cardinality (number of registered routes), deliberately NOT
  per-project/per-engineer, matching CLAUDE.md's non-negotiables. Live-verified: real `curl` (both
  `docker compose exec api curl http://localhost:8000/metrics` and through the internal network)
  returned real Prometheus text with `rpd_http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/healthz",status="200"}`
  incrementing across real requests, plus the full `rpd_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket` histogram.
  **Not** routed through the internet-facing edge (`deploy/nginx/default.conf`, P6-T02-owned, not
  touched) — documented operator instruction: point a Prometheus instance at the `rpd-internal` Docker
  network and scrape `http://api:8000/metrics` directly, never through the public edge/WAF (same
  "internal-only, no need to cross the WAF" posture P6-T01 already chose for MinIO's own console).
- **Worker/solver-worker metrics — documented judgment call, no `/metrics` HTTP endpoint added there.**
  `core/celery_logging.py`'s module docstring spells out why: Celery's default `prefork` pool executes
  tasks in forked CHILD processes, so a naive `start_http_server()` in the parent would always read
  zero (per-process `CollectorRegistry`); `prometheus_client`'s "multiprocess mode" fixes this but adds
  a shared-directory-of-files mechanism, its own small HTTP server, and per-container volume/port
  wiring — judged disproportionate to this task's stated minimal scope ("not expected to stand up a
  full Prometheus+Grafana stack"). Instead: every task emits one structured `task_completed` JSON log
  line (`duration_seconds`) — an operator can already alert/graph on this via log-based metrics tooling
  (Promtail+Loki, `mtail`, etc.) without this app inventing multiprocess Prometheus wiring; flagged as
  a reasonable P7/ops follow-up if dashboards specifically on Celery throughput are wanted.

**Part 3 — backup/restore drill, actually run.**
- `backend/workers/backup_tasks.py` (new): `nightly_pg_dump_backup` — a Celery task on the EXISTING
  general-purpose `worker` app (`workers/worker_app.py`'s `include=[...]`), not a new scheduler/app
  object, per this task's own "reuse if a clean fit" instruction — a nightly `pg_dump` is a background
  job in the same spirit as exports/notifications already on that app, not CP-SAT-scale compute that
  belongs on `solver-worker`'s resource-isolated queue. Runs `pg_dump -Fc` (custom format, via
  `subprocess`, `PGPASSWORD` env var only — never a CLI argument, never logged) against
  `POSTGRES_HOST`/`POSTGRES_PORT`/`POSTGRES_USER`/`POSTGRES_DB`/`POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (the same env vars
  `backend/docker-entrypoint.sh` already assembles `RPD_DATABASE_URL` from), uploads to
  `MinioSettings.backups_bucket` (`rpd-backups`, a bucket SEPARATE from `rpd-exports`, per
  `docs/PROJECT_AND_STACK.md` §6's own "separate bucket, lifecycle-policy retained" wording) under
  `postgres/rpd-{UTC timestamp}.dump`. Never logs `pg_dump`'s raw stderr (only its length) or the
  password.
- `backend/core/minio_config.py`: added `MinioSettings.backups_bucket`/`backup_retention_days` (default
  30 days — §6 doesn't name a number) and `ensure_backups_bucket()`, which idempotently creates the
  bucket AND applies a MinIO lifecycle `Expiration` rule (`minio.lifecycleconfig`) — the "lifecycle-
  policy retained" half of §6's requirement, not just the upload.
- `backend/workers/worker_app.py`: `beat_schedule={"nightly-postgres-backup": {"task": ...,
  "schedule": crontab(hour=2, minute=0)}}` — 02:00 UTC, a quiet-hours default across all three hub
  countries' business hours (Greece/Romania EET/EEST, India IST), operator-overridable.
- `docker-compose.yml`: new `beat` service (`celery -A workers.worker_app beat`, same `backend-image`
  anchor as `api`/`worker`/`solver-worker`) — a separate container from `worker` because Celery beat
  only ever ENQUEUES the task onto `worker`'s own queue, it never executes anything itself. New
  `celerybeat-data` named volume for beat's own schedule-state shelve file (mounted at
  `/var/lib/celery-beat`, chowned to the non-root `appuser` in `backend/Dockerfile` — real bug caught
  and fixed live: Docker auto-creates a missing volume mount target as `root:root`, which the
  non-root `appuser` this image already runs as could not have written into otherwise). Also added
  `RPD_MINIO_BACKUPS_BUCKET`/`RPD_MINIO_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS`/`RPD_LOG_LEVEL` to the shared
  `backend-env` block, and `--config gunicorn_conf.py` to `api`'s command (dropping the now-redundant
  `--access-logfile -`/`--error-logfile -` flags, superseded by that config file).
- `backend/Dockerfile`: added `postgresql-client` (confirmed via `apt-cache`/live `pg_dump --version`
  inside the built image that Debian trixie's package tracks PostgreSQL 17.11, matching
  `postgres:17-alpine` exactly — not assumed) and the `celerybeat-data` mount-point chown fix above.
- `backend/workers/restore_backup.py` (new) + `deploy/backup/restore_from_minio.sh` (new): the restore
  half. Deliberately a MANUAL script (`python -m workers.restore_backup`, wrapped by the shell script
  for `docker compose run`), never a Celery task, since restoring over a database is destructive and
  must always be a human-triggered action, never reachable via `.delay()`/a schedule/an API call. Runs
  `pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner` inside a throwaway container built from the same
  `rpd-backend:latest` image `api`/`worker`/`solver-worker` already use (already has `pg_restore` +
  this app's own configured `RPD_MINIO_*` wiring — no second credential path). `OBJECT_KEY=latest`
  resolves via MinIO's own `last_modified` object metadata (not a lexicographic-key assumption).

  1. Brought up the full 12-container stack (`docker compose up -d --build`) — confirmed
     `docker compose config` still validates first.
  2. Seeded real data (`python -m seed.seed_dev_users` then `seed.seed_demo_data`, run via

  `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` is explicitly named as an accepted, pragmatic allowance by this project's
  own `security-review` skill ("a pragmatic allowance for Tailwind's generated styles and shadcn/ui's
  inline style usage... tighten to a nonce-based policy if a stricter CSP becomes a requirement") — not
  re-scored as a defect here. `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` is a real, if low-residual-risk, gap: it
  removes CSP's value as defense-in-depth against a hypothetical future XSS bug (none currently exists
  — no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, no third-party script origins, no user-content-rendering path found
  anywhere in the SPA). **Final verdict: Medium, formally accepted for this gate (does not block),
  with a concrete, low-risk recommended fix** — since the one inline script is fully static, a
  `script-src 'self' 'sha256-<hash-of-that-exact-script>'` change closes this gap entirely with zero
  runtime risk, and should be picked up as a fast-follow rather than left open indefinitely.
- **New finding (not previously caught):** `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` is present on **every**
  response passing through either WAF container (`waf-api`/`waf-frontend`) — confirmed via a direct
  `curl` to `waf-api:8080` bypassing the edge entirely, and confirmed absent when hitting `api:8000`
  directly (bypassing the WAF) — so this is the `owasp/modsecurity-crs` image's own stock behavior, not
  something P6-T02 configured. My own P6-T02 review had only observed this on the WAF's canned 403
  block page; this session found it also appears on genuine 200/401 application responses carrying real
  data. **Assessed as Low, not higher:** no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header is ever set anywhere in
  the response chain (confirmed on the same real responses), and per the CORS spec a browser will not
  expose a cross-origin response to requesting-page JavaScript without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
  regardless of `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` — so this is inert dead configuration today, not an
  active bypass. It is nonetheless CORS-permissive debt in an app whose entire architecture assumes
  zero cross-origin allowance (same-origin SPA, per the skill's own `connect-src 'self'` design);
  recommend `proxy_hide_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers;` at the edge `nginx` (P6-T02's own file)
  as a cheap, complete fix, tracked non-blocking.

  are an open-redirect and an SSR-hydration issue, and this is a client-only SPA with no SSR anywhere
  (confirmed, not assumed). Both are real, tracked (report-only weekly CI job / documented finding,
  respectively), and **judged Medium, accepted as an interim state for this gate** given the reduced
  exploitability and existing tracking — not escalated to blocking. Recommend the orchestrator open the
  two follow-up tasks P6-T05 already suggested (MinIO version pin + compose re-verification;
  `react-router-dom` v6→v7 migration) at its own discretion, outside this gate.

**Raw SQL string interpolation (CLAUDE.md non-negotiable) — grepped the whole backend fresh, not
assuming prior phases caught every instance:** zero instances of user-reachable f-string/`.format()`/
string-concatenation SQL anywhere in `backend/` outside `alembic/versions/*.py`, where a handful of
`op.execute(f"DROP TRIGGER ... {_CONSTANT_NAME}")`-shaped lines exist — all interpolate only
hardcoded, module-level Python constants (trigger/function/index/enum-type names fixed at migration-
authoring time), never request data or any runtime value; standard, safe Alembic DDL authoring
pattern, not a SQL-injection vector. All ORM-layer queries elsewhere use SQLAlchemy's parameterized
`select(...)`/`.where(...)` construction.

**`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (CLAUDE.md non-negotiable) — grepped the whole `frontend/src` tree fresh:**
zero hits, confirmed again after P5/P6's additions (Scenarios/Versions/Notifications/Export UI) that
weren't in scope for the last time this was checked at this granularity.

**OIDC implementation quality (independent of which IdP it points at, per this task's framing):**
reviewed `backend/core/oidc.py`/`core/config.py::OIDCSettings` in full. `algorithms` defaults to
`["RS256"]` only, `issuer`/`audience` have no default (fail loudly at startup config-load if unset —
can't silently trust an unintended issuer). Token-header `alg` is used only to select the JWK-loading
routine (`PyJWK(signing_key, algorithm=key_algorithm)`); the actual trust decision is
`jwt.decode(..., algorithms=settings.algorithms, ...)`, whose allow-list comes from server-side config
only — a forged header `alg` cannot widen accepted algorithms (this is the classic "alg confusion"
attack class, and it's correctly closed by construction, not by a runtime check that could be
bypassed). `kid`-based key selection with a documented single-key fallback (only when the JWKS document
has exactly one key) — acceptable since signature verification would still fail if the fallback picked
the wrong key; there is never more than one key in practice for a single-issuer JWKS. JWKS is
short-TTL cached per-issuer (picks up IdP key rotation without a request-per-fetch cost). Live-tested:
wrong `aud`/`iss`/expired/tampered-signature/unprovisioned-identity/forged-claims all correctly → 401/
403 as appropriate (see RBAC section above) against a REAL network JWKS fetch this session stood up,
not a monkeypatch — the mechanism is sound and IdP-agnostic exactly as designed. The only open item is
external (`docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` #9 — no confirmed production IdP/app-registration yet) — a known,
tracked, non-code gap, not a defect in this audit's scope, per this task's own framing.

**New findings from live infrastructure testing (not caught by any prior task, since none of them
recreated a running container mid-session or exercised the Docker-level health status):**

1. **WAF-to-`api` upstream DNS staleness (Medium, operational/availability).** After recreating just
   the `api`/`worker`/`solver-worker` containers (to pick up a new OIDC env var — a routine, realistic
   "redeploy the backend" scenario), `GET /api/*` through the edge started returning 502 from
   `waf-api`, with its error log showing `connect() failed (111: Connection refused)` against the
   OLD (pre-recreation) IP address of the `api` service — confirmed via `docker inspect`/`getent hosts`
   that `waf-api`'s embedded-nginx had resolved and cached `api`'s hostname to an IP that no longer
   existed. Restarting only `waf-api` (no other change) immediately fixed it. Root cause: the
   `owasp/modsecurity-crs` image's own nginx config resolves its single `BACKEND` upstream at worker
   -process startup and does not use a `resolver` directive for live re-resolution (the same
   resolver-free pattern P6-T01/P6-T02 documented as "fine... since none of them are scaled up/down
   dynamically" — but a routine single-service redeploy, which is a much more common operation than
   scaling, breaks this assumption). **Impact:** any future redeploy of `api` alone (a normal CI/CD
   rolling update, not just this session's ad hoc env-var change) would silently 502 the ENTIRE API
   surface until an operator notices and manually restarts `waf-api`/`waf-frontend` — a real
   availability gap in the production topology, not a confidentiality/integrity breach, and not
   something P6-T02's own review caught (it never recreated `api` mid-session). **Recommended fix:**
   add a `resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=10s;` + variable-based `proxy_pass` (forces periodic
   re-resolution) to the WAF image's `BACKEND` config, or document/automate that any `api`-only
   redeploy must also bounce `waf-api` (and `waf-frontend` for a `frontend`-only redeploy, same
   mechanism). Tracked as a follow-up, not gate-blocking (availability, not an access-control/data-
   protection failure — the underlying RBAC/encryption/audit controls are all unaffected by this).
2. **Docker `HEALTHCHECK` false-negative on `nginx` (edge) and `frontend` containers (Low-Medium,
   monitoring integrity).** Both containers permanently report `unhealthy` via `docker compose ps`/
   `docker inspect` despite functioning correctly (confirmed real traffic succeeds throughout: `curl`
   through the edge returns 200 for `/`, `/healthz`, `/api/healthz` the entire session). Root cause,
   confirmed live: both containers' `HEALTHCHECK` runs `wget ... http://localhost:<port>/...`, but
   their `/etc/hosts` resolves `localhost` to `::1` (IPv6) and their nginx configs `listen <port>;`
   without an IPv6 equivalent (`listen [::]:<port>;`) — so the healthcheck's own connection is always
   refused (`wget: can't connect to remote host: Connection refused`), while `wget
   http://127.0.0.1:<port>/...` (explicit IPv4) succeeds immediately. **Impact:** any monitoring/
   alerting tooling that keys off Docker's health status (or an orchestrator that restarts unhealthy
   containers) would treat these two permanently-"unhealthy" containers as a standing incident,
   creating exactly the kind of alert fatigue that could mask a REAL future outage — directly relevant
   to this app's own ASVS V7 "reliable error handling/observability" posture that P6-T06 was built to
   establish. **Recommended fix:** either add `listen [::]:<port>;` to both nginx configs, or change
   the `HEALTHCHECK`/generator scripts to probe `127.0.0.1` explicitly instead of `localhost`
   (`frontend/Dockerfile` line 86; the edge `nginx` container's Compose-level healthcheck). Tracked as
   a follow-up, not gate-blocking (does not affect any access-control/data-protection/confidentiality
   control — purely a monitoring-signal defect).
3. **`Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` on every WAF-proxied response (Low, CORS-hygiene debt) — see
   CSP/headers section above for full detail.** Refines P6-T02's own Info-level observation (which had
   only seen this on the WAF's block page) to: this header is present on EVERY response through either
   WAF container, including genuine 200/401 application responses. Inert today (no
   `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is ever set), not gate-blocking, but real configuration debt worth a
   one-line `proxy_hide_header` fix at the edge.
4. **Minor working-tree hygiene (Info).** `secrets/*.txt` and `deploy/tls/dev/{server.crt,server.key}`
   were already present in the working tree at the start of this session (left over from a prior P6
   task's testing rather than torn down) — correctly `.gitignore`d, `chmod 600`, and every file is
   explicitly self-documented as dev-only, so this is not a security defect, just inconsistent with
   the meticulous "tear down every throwaway artifact" precedent every other P6 task/review set. No
   action needed beyond noting it.
